newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Indonesia says Cambodia ASEAN entry set for July.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia says Cambodia ASEAN entry set for July.

text.p: Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas has told Cambodian leaders their country will be admitted to the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) in July, a Cambodian official said on Tuesday.

"It is confirmed. We will be an ASEAN member by July," co-Minister of the Council of Ministers Sok An told reporters after meeting including Alatas, Indonesian President Suharto and Cambodian co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen.
Sok An said Alatas gave the co-premiers the news in a briefing on the ASEAN-European Union meeting in Singapore last week.

The announcement appears to indicate two other would-be members, Laos and Burma, would be admitted in July as the grouping celebrates its 30th anniversary. ASEAN had said all three would be admitted simultaneously.
ASEAN currently links Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
Suharto, who last visited Cambodia in 1968, is on a tour of all three would-be member nations with businessmen and officials.

When asked to confirm Sok An's announcement, co-Minister of the Council of Ministers Veng Sereyvuth told Reuters, "It is not wrong," but added that Alatas alone could not confirm Cambodia's membership as "his is just one country (in ASEAN)".
However ASEAN analysts said the informal announcement confirmed what for Cambodia has been a foregone conclusion.

Kao Kim Hourn, director of the Cambodian Institute for Cooperation and Peace think-tank, noted that Cambodia was already preparing to open an embassy in June in Malaysia, which would be lead member of ASEAN when Cambodia joined, and had set aside the $1 million ASEAN membership fee.
Some analysts had worried that political conflicts between Ranariddh and Hun Sen, who formed an uneasy coalition following U.N.-run elections in 1993, might delay Phnom Penh's entry into ASEAN.

Suharto's visit to Cambodia came on the heels of government tensions that led to clashes in the northwest, but Sok An said the co-premiers had emphasised the country's stability in the meeting with the Indonesian president.

"Everywhere, in every country, you have some technical problems. But what is important here is that the two parties have the same idea... to maintain the political stability, to strengthen the national unity," he said.
But King Norodom Sihanouk was more blunt as he gave Suharto a tour of the famous Silver Pagoda in the palace grounds after the morning talks with the co-premiers.
Remarking on Cambodia's religious community, Sihanouk told Suharto that Cambodia had "very good, peaceful co-existence... The only problems we have are between Khmer and Khmer."

Despite tensions, Indonesia has apparently given Cambodia full support for ASEAN entry, and the two nations strengthened ties by signing a trade pact, an exchange of notes on the establishment of a joint commission and a memorandum of understanding on oil and gas exploration and production.
Sok An said the trade pact would boost Indonesian imports of Cambodian soya and rice and increase trade, now worth about $10 to $15 million per year.

The oil and gas agreement between Cambodia and Pertamina, Indonesia's state-owned oil and gas company, provides for the exchange of human resources and technical information, the Ministry of Industry said in a statement.
The statement said the agreement would accelerate the development of the oil and gas sector in Cambodia.
